title: Blank Column Entries

illustrates.quote: Use guide dots across the width of a column to indicate a blank space or a blank to be filled in. Explain the series of guide dots in a transcriber's note. (See ... Sample 11-11: Blank Column Entries on page 11-36.)

print.caption: Table 13 / Trends in Availability of Drugs by 12th Graders / Percentage saying “fairly easy” or “very easy” to get
print.notes: Several cells are blank in print because that survey question was not asked/reported in earlier years (e.g. no 1986 data at all for Amy/butyl nitrites, PCP, or Ecstasy; no 1986-1988 data for Ecstasy).
print.printFeatures: Bordered box; two-line bold centered title above the box, italic subtitle line ("Percentage saying...") beneath the title; header row (years) bold with ruled line beneath; row headings left-aligned, some wrapping to two lines ("Amy/butyl nitrites", "Some other hallucinogen", "Ecstasy (MDMA)").

braille.notes: Line 1 carries the transcriber's-note continuation marker '#,-' at the right margin of the top box line. A transcriber's note (lines 9-10) explains: "A series of dot #es acr [across] a width [of a] column indicates a blank space." Each blank print cell is rendered as a run of dot-5 guide dots (shaded grey in the PDF sample image) across that column's width, e.g. the 1986 cells for Amy/butyl nitrites, PCP, and Ecstasy, and the 1986-1988 cells for Ecstasy.

resolution: print.headers' first cell resolved to '' (blank above the drug-name row headings in print, confirmed against the PDF image, p. 318), not a fabricated '(drug)' placeholder.
